passage: My name is Joseph, and I live across the landing from Dolma, so I hear her door more often than I see her. Before the baby came, she would stop to chat about her balcony plants. For weeks afterwards the door stayed shut, and the plants went brown. One evening we met by the lift. She was holding the baby carefully, the way you hold something that might break, and her face was blank. "Everyone says these are the best days," she said quietly. "I feel nothing. And at night I keep imagining something terrible happening to her." I'm no expert, and I couldn't tell what was really going on inside her. I said, "You're not a bad mother. That sounds heavy. Would you tell your doctor exactly what you just told me?" Her husband, Tsering, took her the next week. Now she sees a counsellor too. Yesterday I saw her watering new plants.

qa.q: Where does Joseph live in relation to Dolma?
qa.a: Joseph lives across the landing from Dolma.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when she met Joseph by the lift?
qa.a: Dolma felt numb and empty, and frightened at night; she said she felt nothing and kept imagining something terrible happening to the baby.

qa.q: Which choice did Joseph make at the lift, and why did it help?
qa.a: Joseph told Dolma she was not a bad mother and suggested telling her doctor exactly what she had said, which turned a hidden feeling into a step toward proper help.

qa.q: What would change if Joseph had replied, "Cheer up, these are the best days"?
qa.a: Dolma might have felt more alone and ashamed, and could have kept her numbness and dread hidden instead of reaching her doctor.

Week three. At two in the morning Jaya stood over the cot again, one hand hovering near the baby's chest. She had checked on him eleven times since midnight. When he slept, she lay awake with her heart racing, telling herself a good mother should feel grateful, not scared.
Week five. Her younger sister Aditi arrived with a tiffin of idlis and found Jaya crying over a pile of tiny clothes. "Some days I don't even want to hold him," Jaya whispered. "What kind of mother says that?" Aditi sat down beside her. "A tired one who needs help. This isn't your fault." That afternoon Aditi took her to the doctor, who listened carefully, said this happens to many new parents and gets better with help, and arranged regular sessions with a counsellor.
Week nine. The nights were still hard. But when the baby grabbed her plait, Jaya laughed, and the dread came less often.

passage: The rain had knocked the power out again, and the fan above the cot hung still. Arohi sat on the bed beside her five-week-old son and felt nothing at all. Not love, not even tiredness, just a flat grey hum. For three weeks she had been waking at four with her heart racing, sure something terrible was about to happen to him, and then lying there unable to lift him. Her friend Dolma arrived dripping, carrying a flask of soup, and found the baby crying while Arohi stared at the wall. 'I'm a bad mother,' Arohi whispered. Dolma knelt beside her. 'You're a tired, unwell one. That's different, and it can get better.' The roads were flooding, so Dolma rang the clinic from her phone, booked the doctor's first slot for the next morning, and stayed the night so Arohi could sleep.

passage: At the vaccination clinic in their Pune colony, Sharmila held her daughter so tightly that the baby squirmed. She had not slept more than an hour at a stretch for weeks, and not because the baby woke. She lay listening to the tiny breaths, certain they would stop the moment she closed her eyes. She had stopped answering her sister's calls and ate standing at the counter, if she ate at all. When the nurse, Jaya, asked, 'And how is Amma doing?', Sharmila opened her mouth to say fine and started crying instead. 'I keep thinking something awful will happen. I should be enjoying her.' Jaya pulled up a stool. 'Many new mothers go through this, and it is not your fault. It's something doctors treat.' Before Sharmila left, Jaya had walked her down the corridor and booked her a slot with the clinic doctor that same afternoon.

qa.q: Where did Sharmila take her daughter?
qa.a: To the vaccination clinic in their Pune colony.

qa.q: Why was Sharmila unable to sleep, and what was she feeling?
qa.a: She was terrified and anxious that her baby's breaths would stop if she closed her eyes, a worry that had gone on for weeks.

qa.q: How did Jaya's response help Sharmila?
qa.a: Jaya listened, said it was not Sharmila's fault and that doctors treat it, and booked a doctor's slot that same afternoon so help did not depend on Sharmila finding the energy later.

qa.q: What would change if Jaya had only asked about the baby's vaccines?
qa.a: Sharmila might have said 'fine' and gone home still frightened and alone, with the worry continuing to eat into her days and her eating.

grounding: Shows a new mother's lasting intrusive worry disrupting sleep, eating and contact with family, and a nurse who treats it as a health matter and connects her to a doctor.

passage:
'You haven't touched your tea, Leela.'
'I'm not thirsty. Disha, can I tell you something awful?'
'Always.'
'When he cries, I hand him to Mum. I don't want to hold him. It's like I'm watching all of this from behind glass.'
'How long has it been like this?'
'Since the second week. That's two months now. Everyone says the baby blues pass. Mine haven't.'
'Have you told the doctor?'
'My check-up is Thursday. I was going to cancel. What if she thinks I'm a terrible mother?'
'Leela, look at me. Feeling like this doesn't make you a bad mother. It means you need care, the same as healing after the stitches did. Doctors see this often, and it gets better with the right help.'
'Will you come with me?'
'I'll drive you. And tonight I'm doing the two o'clock feed so you can sleep.'

qa.q: When is Leela's check-up?
qa.a: Thursday.

qa.q: What does Leela's plan to cancel the check-up suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels ashamed and afraid of being judged as a terrible mother, even though she has been struggling for two months.

qa.q: Which of Disha's replies helped most, and why?
qa.a: Comparing it to healing after the stitches, then offering to drive and do the night feed, took away the blame and made getting care feel practical.

qa.q: What would change if Disha had said, 'All new mums feel that, it'll pass'?
qa.a: Leela might have cancelled Thursday's check-up and kept feeling cut off from her baby, believing she just had to wait it out alone.

grounding: Shows a new mother whose detachment from her baby has lasted for months, and a friend who frames it as a health need and helps her keep the doctor's appointment.

passage: When my son was two months old, I, Vandana, was still waiting to feel what the other mothers described. Instead I felt numb. I fed him, changed him, rocked him, and felt as if I was watching someone else do it. At night I lay awake with a loop of terrible what-ifs: he'd stop breathing, I'd drop him on the stairs. I stopped answering calls. I told myself I was just a bad mother. My friend Uma visited and found me staring at the wall while the baby cried. She held my hand and said, 'This isn't you failing. This is something a doctor can help with.' She came with me to my doctor that week. I'm getting support now, and slowly I feel him as mine.

qa.a: She felt numb and detached, as if watching someone else, and was haunted by frightening what-ifs.
